clue.text: Barometer's main location, where pilot views computerized data (12, two words)

parts.note: the glass is the household name for a barometer
a cockpit is the arena where the main action takes place, as in the cockpit of Europe

explanation.surface: A weather-minded owner wonders where the barometer belongs, while a pilot studies screens of data.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s is possessive in the surface but simply joins the two pieces in the wordplay: the barometer's main place.
explanation.definitionFit: Modern aircraft whose instruments are electronic screens rather than dials are said to have this kind of flight deck.

clue.text: ME hotspot capturing hearts with line in amatory verse form?

indicators.note: capturing means taking prisoner, so the place name holds the cards suit letter inside it

parts.note: Gaza is a flashpoint in the Middle East (ME)
H is the abbreviation for hearts in card games
L is the abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: A trouble spot in the Middle East wins hearts with a line of love poetry.
explanation.walkthrough: Hearts suggests romance to match the amatory verse, but it is just the card-suit letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The ghazal is a Persian and Urdu lyric form of rhyming couplets, traditionally about love and longing.

clue.text: Monastery suffering malaise with resident artist

indicators.note: a resident lives inside, so the artist goes within the shuffled letters
suffering means in a bad way, so the letters of the ailment word are disturbed

parts.note: taken as written
RA, Royal Academician, is the usual crossword artist

explanation.surface: A monastery is going through a bad spell, with an artist living there.
explanation.definitionFit: A lamaserai is a Tibetan Buddhist monastery of lamas, so it is a kind of religious house.

clue.text: US police unit raised strap delivering sharp blow

parts.note: first meaning: the American special weapons and tactics squad

indicators.note: in a down clue raised means lifted upwards, so the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: taws is a leather strap once used to punish Scottish schoolchildren
second meaning: a smart slap, as at a fly

explanation.surface: An American police squad lifts a leather strap and lands a stinging blow.
explanation.walkthrough: Two definitions sandwich a reversal; all three routes lead to the same four letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The acronym names the armed police team, and the ordinary word means a smart slap with something flat.

clue.text: Up, not down with old cloth shoe!

indicators.note: in a down clue Up means the pieces are written from the bottom upwards

parts.note: taken as written
a bas is the French cry meaning down with

explanation.surface: A protest chant: up with this, not down with that old canvas shoe!
explanation.walkthrough: Up, not down sounds like a slogan; Up is the reversal signal and down with is the French protest cry a bas.
explanation.definitionFit: Chambers records the sabaton as a broad-toed shoe of the sixteenth century as well as the armoured foot covering of a suit of armour.

clue.text: Supposed energy in credo of eccentric?

indicators.note: eccentric means off-centre and odd, so the letters before it are thrown out of order

parts.note: both words taken as written

explanation.surface: An oddball's creed rests on some imagined energy.
explanation.walkthrough: Credo of eccentric reads as a crank's belief; of is part of the letters to rearrange, not a joining word.
explanation.definitionFit: Baron von Reichenbach proposed od as a hypothetical force pervading nature, never shown to exist, hence supposed.

clue.text: 'I loved Duncan' — by which Macbeth might have hanged?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Edward Gordon ..., the stage designer who was the dancer Isadora Duncan's lover

definitions.text: by which Macbeth might have hanged?
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the Scots word for the neck

explanation.walkthrough: Duncan and Macbeth summon the Scottish play, but this Duncan is Isadora, the dancer; the hanging is by the neck, in Scots.
explanation.definitionFit: Gordon Craig had a famous affair with Isadora Duncan, and craig is Scots for the neck, which a hanged man hangs by.

clue.text: Exchange of gifts, not quite enough for rich peasant

indicators.note: falling just short means the word is cut off a letter before its end

parts.note: a kulak was a prosperous peasant farmer in Russia

explanation.surface: Swapping presents does not quite add up to enough to make a peasant rich.
explanation.definitionFit: The kula is the ceremonial exchange of shell valuables among the Trobriand Islanders, studied by Malinowski.

clue.text: A groom

parts.note: surface reading: a plain description of a stable servant
setter's reading: there is no wordplay here, because this is the competition word for which solvers write their own clue

explanation.walkthrough: Azed's competition puzzles give the prize word only a bare definition; competitors send in their own cryptic clue for it.
explanation.definitionFit: This archaic word for a stable servant comes from the palfrey, the riding horse he looked after.

clue.text: Copshop or equivalent for half a dozen coppahs once?
One formerly i/c fences etc, firm about diversion of way

indicators.note: about means around, so one word is wrapped around the other

parts.note: firm and hard are synonyms

indicators.note: a diversion sends traffic off its normal route, so the letters of the word that follows are rerouted

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A historical note about an official once responsible for fences, whose firm objected to a footpath being diverted.
explanation.definitionFit: A hayward was the manorial officer who looked after hedges and fences and kept stray cattle off the crops; i/c means in charge of.

clue.text: Something seen in Peru, an accessory…for gauchos?

parts.note: surface padding that sets up the riddle of what was spotted

indicators.note: something seen in a phrase is visible inside it, spread across its word boundaries

parts.note: the letters run across the end of Peru, the whole of an and the start of accessory

explanation.surface: A traveller's note about some garment spotted in Peru that gauchos might wear.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition shares words with the letters it hides, so the clue doubles back on itself; the ellipsis and question mark flag that a ruana is only loosely a gaucho's accessory.
explanation.definitionFit: A ruana is a woollen poncho-like wrap worn in the Andes, the sort of outer garment a South American horseman would wear.

clue.text: Fixed hooks I dispensed with before execution?

indicators.note: before places the shortened word ahead of the next piece
dispensed with means done without, so the single letter is removed

parts.note: unci is the plural of uncus, Latin for a hook, used in anatomy
taken as written, the letter to drop
hanging is a form of execution

explanation.surface: A prisoner's hooks were fixed in place and done away with just before the execution.
explanation.definitionFit: Something fixed stays the same and does not alter, so it is unchanging; the adjectives are synonyms.

clue.text: Bud Flanagan initially touring Spain with his partner — what's happened?

indicators.note: to tour a place is to go round it, so those letters circle another
initially points to the first letter of each of the preceding words

parts.note: the first letters of the comedian's two names
E is the international vehicle code for Spain (España)
Chesney Allen was Bud Flanagan's stage partner

explanation.surface: A music-hall comic goes on tour in Spain with his partner, and someone asks what has gone on.
explanation.walkthrough: Flanagan and Allen were a British music-hall double act of the 1930s to 1950s, part of the Crazy Gang.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that has befallen has happened or come about, so the past participle answers the question of what has occurred.

clue.text: Pet, one in New Zealand, must return for ulcer treatment

indicators.note: to return is to go back, so the whole string is read from right to left

parts.note: a cat is a typical pet

indicators.note: in places the single item inside the two letters for the country

parts.note: the standard abbreviation for New Zealand
one as the article a

explanation.surface: A vet's note: a pet in New Zealand has to come back for ulcer treatment.
explanation.walkthrough: The pet is wordplay only; the definition is the last two words, so the pet's ulcer is a red herring.
explanation.definitionFit: Zantac is a brand name of ranitidine, a drug long prescribed to reduce stomach acid and heal ulcers.

clue.text: Smarties making caries rampant in all quarters but one?

indicators.note: rampant means running wild, so the letters are set loose into a new order
but one means all except one, so a single compass letter is left out

parts.note: taken as written
the four quarters are the compass points north, south, east and west

explanation.surface: A dentist's lament: Smarties sweets are spreading tooth decay almost everywhere.
explanation.walkthrough: Smarties are a chocolate sweet in Britain, which fits caries; here the word means know-alls. North is the quarter dropped.
explanation.definitionFit: Smarties, like smart alecks, are people who think themselves clever, which is what wiseacres are.

clue.text: Spectators may be seen showing pert ——s off here?

definitions.text: Spectators may be seen showing pert ——s off here?

parts.words: Spectators may be seen showing pert ——s off here?
parts.note: surface reading: a racecourse where smart racegoers parade and show themselves off
setter's reading: the blank is the answer itself used as a common noun, a kind of broad neck scarf, so the venue and the neckwear share one name

explanation.walkthrough: Royal Ascot is the English race meeting famous for its fashion parade; the same name is given to a wide cravat, which fills the blank.
explanation.definitionFit: The racecourse in Berkshire is the place where fashionably dressed spectators go to be seen, cravats included.

clue.text: Back exposure following strange gray pigmentation, unnatural

indicators.note: following places the reversed piece after the rearranged one
something strange is out of its usual form, so the colour word is rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: back tells you to read the word for exposure in the opposite direction

parts.note: to air something is to expose it, and exposure to view is an airing

explanation.surface: A medical note about a patient's back, exposed and showing an odd grey pigmentation.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes Back a body part; it is the reversal signal, and the definition is the last two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Argyria is a blue-grey discoloration of the skin caused by silver compounds building up in the body, an unnatural colouring.

clue.text: Oven 50% cooler around end of lunch

indicators.note: around means the shortened word is wrapped about the single letter
half of the word is dropped and only its second half is used

parts.note: taken as written before halving

indicators.note: end of means the final letter of the following word

parts.note: the last letter of lunch

explanation.surface: Someone notes an oven running half as hot as usual around the end of lunchtime.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the back half of cooler is kept, and the end of lunch slips between its last two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A lehr is the long kiln in which newly made glass is annealed, so it is a specialised industrial oven.

clue.text: Goals I put past keeper heading up round rim subtly

indicators.note: put past means placed after, so the single letter goes at the end
in a down clue heading up means travelling upwards, so the word reads backwards
round means surrounding, so the reversed word encloses the shuffled one

parts.note: a keepnet holds an angler's catch, so a net is a keeper

indicators.note: subtly suggests craftily rearranged, so the letters of the edge word are shuffled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A football scene: a striker heads the ball past the goalkeeper, glancing it in off the rim.
explanation.walkthrough: Goals and keeper conjure football, but the keeper is a net and goals means ends or destinations.
explanation.definitionFit: Termini are end points, and a goal is the end towards which one travels, so the plurals match.

clue.text: Scottish grease to soften belt up

parts.note: to cree is to soften grain by boiling it
belt up is British slang for be quiet, and sh is the call for silence

explanation.surface: Instructions to work a Scottish grease into a leather belt to make it supple.
explanation.walkthrough: Belt looks like the strap being greased, but belt up is one phrase meaning shut up.
explanation.definitionFit: Creesh is the Scots word for grease or fat, as a noun and as a verb meaning to oil.

clue.text: Have a drink? (Menial fills the lady up)

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the whole is read from bottom to top
to fill something is to occupy its inside, so the servant word goes within

parts.note: her is the pronoun for a lady
a serf is a lowly bonded labourer

explanation.surface: A servant tops up the lady's glass and asks if she will have a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: Fills the lady up reads as pouring her a drink; it means the servant goes inside her and the lot is turned over.
explanation.definitionFit: To refresh oneself is to take refreshment, often a drink; the question mark admits the loose fit.

clue.text: Entry arranged one's taken in to receive instruction in poesy

indicators.note: taken in means admitted inside, so the single letter goes within the reshuffled word
arranged means put into a new order, so the word before it is reshuffled

parts.note: taken as written
one as the article a

explanation.surface: A note on an entry being put together so that someone can be taught the art of poetry.
explanation.walkthrough: In poesy marks the answer as a poet's form: Spenser spells train this way.
explanation.definitionFit: Trayne is Spenser's spelling of train, and to train can mean to undergo instruction.

clue.text: Poet's taunt under control with women involved

indicators.note: involved means caught up inside, so the women's letter sits within

parts.note: tight control is firm control, as in a tight rein
W is the abbreviation for women

explanation.surface: A poet keeps his barbs in check when women are present.
explanation.walkthrough: Poet's marks a word from Spenser, whose twight is a form of twit.
explanation.definitionFit: To twit someone is to taunt or tease them, and Spenser spelt the verb twight.

clue.text: Lop ends off part of garden shed that's wrong way round

indicators.note: the stretch found is to be read in the opposite direction
part of tells you the letters are a stretch lying inside the next words

parts.note: the letters straddle the end of garden and the start of shed

explanation.surface: A gardener is told to trim the ends off part of a shed that was put up facing the wrong way.
explanation.walkthrough: Lop ends off reads like an instruction to remove outer letters, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Sned is a dialect verb meaning to prune or cut off branches, which is lopping.

clue.text: Distinctive hairstyle, sadder when cut

indicators.note: cut up means chopped into bits, so the letters are shuffled and reassembled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone with a distinctive hairstyle feels gloomier once it has been cut off.
explanation.walkthrough: Cut looks like a haircut, which fits the scene; here it is the signal to chop up the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Dreads is the short form of dreadlocks, the matted rope-like locks associated with Rastafarians.

clue.text: Navy cutting waterproof gear is bewildering

indicators.note: something cutting into another piece sits inside it

parts.note: waders are waterproof boots reaching up the legs, worn by anglers
N is the abbreviation for navy

explanation.surface: Someone finds it baffling that the navy has cut its waterproof clothing.
explanation.definitionFit: In an older transitive sense, to wander someone is to confuse or bewilder them, so the verb in the third person means is bewildering.

clue.text: Duck eggs (German) with beginning of ducks inside

indicators.note: inside means placed within, so that letter goes into the German word

parts.note: Eier is German for eggs

indicators.note: beginning of means the first letter of the next word

parts.note: the first letter of ducks

explanation.surface: A German recipe: duck with eggs, and some ducks inside.
explanation.definitionFit: The eider is a large northern sea duck, prized for the soft down of its nest.

clue.text: Minor e.g. frequently holding voice back

indicators.note: holding means the abbreviation contains the next piece

parts.note: fr. is a dictionary abbreviation for frequently

indicators.note: back means the word for voice is turned to read the other way

parts.note: to air a view is to voice it

explanation.surface: Reads as grammar or music: a minor key, say, often holding a voice part back.
explanation.walkthrough: Minor looks like a musical key or a child; the Friars Minor are the Franciscans, so one of them is a Minor.
explanation.definitionFit: A Franciscan is called a Friar Minor, so a Minor is an example of a mendicant brother.

clue.text: Brave following one, brave's traditional enemy — not half!

indicators.note: not half means one of the two halves of the word is thrown away
the half kept is the one that comes after, so the front half goes

parts.note: in Western films the traditional foe of a Native American warrior is the paleface, the white settler

explanation.surface: A Western scene: a brave follows his old enemy, and not half.
explanation.walkthrough: Not half sounds like the British slang for very much indeed; here it literally halves the word.
explanation.definitionFit: To brave something and to face it both mean to confront it with courage.

clue.text: Base for Olympic Airlines flight (as earlier)

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the country where the Greek national airline was based
second meaning: an obsolete word for a flight of steps

explanation.walkthrough: Flight looks like an air journey to go with the airline, but it is a flight of stairs; as earlier marks that sense as archaic.
explanation.definitionFit: Olympic Airlines was the flag carrier of the country, and the same spelling once meant a staircase or set of steps.

clue.text: Outside stone shed, sitting in perfect place

indicators.note: outside says the letters to lose are the outer ones at each end
to shed is to cast off, so those letters are removed

parts.note: st is the abbreviation for stone, the British weight of 14 pounds
sedent is an old word meaning seated

explanation.surface: Someone sitting outside by a cast-off stone in an idyllic spot.
explanation.walkthrough: Shed looks like a garden building beside the stone; it is a verb meaning cast off.
explanation.definitionFit: The garden of Eden is the biblical paradise, so the name stands for any ideal place.

clue.text: It's protein and extracted from (say) liver I eat, secreting one

indicators.note: secreting means hiding away, so the single item is tucked inside
extracted from means the word before it is pulled out of the organ word

parts.note: the liver is an example of a gland
taken as written, the letters to be removed

indicators.note: say marks liver as only an example, of the class of organ that is needed

parts.note: taken as written
one as the article a
to dine is to eat

explanation.surface: A dietary note: there is protein to be had from liver, which the speaker eats.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes and an ordinary conjunction, but it is the string taken out of gland. Then I and dine sandwich the single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Gliadin, also spelt with a final E, is one of the proteins of wheat gluten.

clue.text: Architectural arc, rising in height formerly, not used nowadays

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the haunch of an arch, the curve near its springing

definitions.text: rising in height formerly, not used nowadays
definitions.meaning: second meaning: an obsolete verb meaning to raise or lift up, now replaced by enhance

explanation.walkthrough: Formerly and not used nowadays both flag the second sense as obsolete; enhance is its surviving descendant.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names the curved lower part of an arch and is also an old form meaning to raise higher.

clue.text: Blindly submissive sign of assent about time of day

indicators.note: about means around, so the gesture word wraps the old word for a time

parts.note: a nod signals agreement
sele is an old word for time or season

explanation.surface: Someone nods along to whatever time is named, doing as they are told without question.
explanation.walkthrough: Sele (also seel) is an archaic word for a time or season; it sits between the first two and last letters of the gesture.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone led by the nose follows another unquestioningly, which is the idiom behind this adjective.

clue.text: Unruly heir's in ski resort before start of season, being flashy?

indicators.note: before puts the resort and its contents ahead of the final letter
in places the reshuffled letters inside the resort's name

parts.note: Tignes is a ski resort in the French Alps

indicators.note: unruly means not keeping order, so the letters that follow are reshuffled

parts.note: taken as written, apostrophe dropped

indicators.note: start of points to the first letter of the next word

parts.note: the first letter of season

explanation.surface: A badly behaved rich heir shows off at a ski resort before the season begins.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram lands inside the resort, splitting it after its third letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiger was slang for a flashily dressed swaggerer, so tigerish can mean showy; the question mark admits the stretch.
